description: SIRIUS is a student team interested in aerospace, physics, engineering, software, AI, and space exploration. We want to build a practical and technically meaningful solution using NASA data and technologies. Our interests include planetary exploration, spacecraft and mission design, astronomy, Earth and space science, and interactive software. We are looking for curious teammates interested in coding and engineering.
summary:
At the Moon's south pole, the Sun and Earth both sit right on the horizon. A small hill or a few days of launch delay can leave a lander with no power or no radio contact. NASA has tools that can work this out, but they are slow to use when you need to compare many options.

We built the Lunar Landing Site Navigator to make that comparison quick. You pick a landing site and a date, and the app shows where the Sun and Earth are in the local sky, how many hours of sunlight and Earth contact you get, and when both happen together. Our "What if we slip?" planner checks every arrival date in the next 12 months and shows which ones still work.

It matters because mission schedules change often. Planners need fast answers, and students and the public deserve a clear way to see why landing at the pole is so hard.
details:
What it does

The Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app for comparing lunar landing sites and dates. You choose a past or planned landing site, such as Apollo 11, Chandrayaan-3 or IM-2, or click anywhere on a 3D Moon to set your own point. Then you set a landing time.

How it works

The app shows the Sun and Earth against the local horizon and follows their paths over a full lunar day. It reports the solar elevation, the time left until sunset and Earthset, and the hours of sunlight, Earth contact and both together. You can play time forward like a film and compare several sites and dates side by side.

At the south pole a mountain can hide the Sun completely, so for six polar sites we built real skylines from NASA LOLA elevation data. You can switch between a smooth Moon and real terrain to see how much the landscape changes the result.

Key feature: "What if we slip?"

Launch delays are normal, so the user enters a mission length and the app scans 365 arrival dates in under two seconds. A calendar marks the dates that keep power and contact for the whole mission.

Benefits and impact

- Mission planners can re-check a site or date in seconds when the schedule changes.

- Science and engineering teams can look at the same clear picture.

- Students, teachers and the public can see why landing at the pole is so hard.

Accuracy

We compared 100 Sun and Earth positions against NASA JPL Horizons, and the largest difference was about 0.01 degrees. The full table is in the app, next to an open list of what the model leaves out.

Tools and technologies

- React and Three.js: the app and the 3D Moon

- Astronomy Engine: Sun, Earth and Moon positions

- NASA JPL Horizons: accuracy check

- NASA LOLA: real terrain skylines

- NASA LRO imagery: the Moon's surface

- OpenAI Codex and Claude: help with planning, code and testing

Creative elements

- Planner mode gives exact angles and UTC times, and Explain mode says the same thing in plain sentences.

- The sky view draws the Sun and Earth at their true size against the horizon.

- Every result is labelled as smooth Moon or real terrain, so the user always knows what they are looking at.
